the-modern-ai-agent-2023.name: The modern AI agent
the-modern-ai-agent-2023.definition: A software system built on a large language model that perceives its environment, reasons over open-ended tasks, and acts through tools in a loop.
the-modern-ai-agent-2023.bottleneck: Before the modern AI agent, machines could not perceive, reason over, and act on open-ended tasks in a loop, because no model could flexibly convert between language, perception and action, and there was no practical way to train or steer such a model.

transformer-architecture-2017.name: Transformer architecture
transformer-architecture-2017.definition: A neural network architecture based entirely on self-attention, dispensing with recurrence and convolutions, that became the foundation of modern large language models.
transformer-architecture-2017.bottleneck: Before Transformer architecture, training sequence models on long contexts was impossible or impractical because recurrent networks processed tokens sequentially and could not be parallelized.

verification.notes: Date 2017 and causal arrow to 2023 agents check out, and Q2/Q3 hold: post-2017 frontier models are overwhelmingly Transformer-based. Q1 is overstated, however: RNN/LSTM systems (GNMT) already did production translation and parallel convolutional rivals (ByteNet 2016, ConvS2S 2017) were concurrent, so the Transformer was a large efficiency/quality improvement, not the removal of an impossibility; Q2 independently carries the gate.

stored-program-architecture-1945.name: Stored-program architecture
stored-program-architecture-1945.definition: The von Neumann design in which instructions and data share one memory, making the computer a universal, reprogrammable machine.
stored-program-architecture-1945.bottleneck: Before the stored-program architecture, general-purpose computation was impractical because machines had to be physically rewired or reconfigured for each new task.

sources.title: First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC

verification.notes: Date 1945 (First Draft on EDVAC) is correct and strictly before the parent, and Q2/Q3 hold for mainstream computing. Weakness is priority/authorship: Eckert (Jan 1944 memo) and Mauchly had the design before von Neumann, Turing's 1936 universal machine and Zuse's 1936 patents anticipated stored instructions, so sole attribution to the 1945 report is disputed; also ENIAC was already general-purpose, making Q1 an impracticality claim rather than impossibility.

cross-entropy-loss-1948.name: Cross-entropy loss
cross-entropy-loss-1948.definition: The measure of divergence between a predicted probability distribution and the true one, derived from Shannon entropy and used as the standard training objective for classifiers and language models.
cross-entropy-loss-1948.bottleneck: Before cross-entropy loss, scoring a predicted distribution against reality was impossible or impractical because there was no principled loss measuring distributional mismatch for training classifiers.

verification.notes: Q2/Q3 hold: cross-entropy is in fact the GPT-class pre-training objective. Weakness is dating/naming: Shannon 1948 introduced entropy (and a relative-entropy quantity), but 'cross-entropy' as a named two-distribution loss and training objective crystallized later (Kullback-Leibler 1951 and after), and the evaluator's own Q1 was only partial, so the 1948 label is anachronistic though the underlying quantity is present.

word2vec-embeddings-2013.name: Word2vec embeddings
word2vec-embeddings-2013.definition: Efficient methods for learning dense word vectors from raw text in which semantic similarity becomes geometric proximity.
word2vec-embeddings-2013.bottleneck: Before word2vec embeddings, representing word meaning for computation was impossible or impractical at scale because sparse count-based vectors were high-dimensional and training neural word vectors was slow.

sources.title: Efficient Estimation of Word Representations in Vector Space

verification.notes: Date 2013 correct and Q2 holds (wide transfer and adoption). Weaknesses: Q1 and Q3 were only partial in evaluation, embeddings already existed via Bengio 2003, and GloVe (2014) was a near-simultaneous substitute reaching comparable vectors from co-occurrence counts, so necessity attaches to scalable embeddings generally, not word2vec uniquely; its line to Transformers is also indirect since Transformers learn their own embeddings.

cuda-2007.name: CUDA
cuda-2007.definition: NVIDIA's parallel computing platform that opened GPU hardware to general-purpose computation through a C-like programming model.
cuda-2007.bottleneck: Before CUDA, using GPU parallelism for general computation was impossible or impractical because graphics hardware could only be programmed through graphics APIs not designed for it.

verification.notes: Date 2007 (CUDA 1.0, Feb 2007) correct and Q2/Q3 hold for frontier training on NVIDIA/CUDA. Q1 is overstated: GPGPU was already possible via shader hacks and BrookGPU (2004, by CUDA lead Ian Buck), and AMD's Close-to-Metal/Stream (2006) was a concurrent alternative platform, so CUDA removed impracticality rather than impossibility and the time was partly ripe.

gradient-descent-1847.name: Gradient descent
gradient-descent-1847.definition: A first-order iterative optimization algorithm for finding a local minimum of a differentiable function, rooted in Cauchy's 1847 method.
gradient-descent-1847.bottleneck: Before gradient descent, minimizing a complex function was impractical because there was no general iterative rule that used local slope information to improve a solution step by step.

verification.notes: Cauchy 1847 date is correct and Q2 holds: gradient methods do train essentially all neural networks. Weakness: independent rediscovery/formalization followed (Hadamard 1907, Curry 1944, Robbins-Monro stochastic approximation 1951), and Newton's method and least squares predated it, so Q3 necessity for this specific 1847 formulation is downgraded; the evaluator already scored Q3 only partial.

linnainmaa-s-automatic-differentiation-1.name: Linnainmaa's automatic differentiation
linnainmaa-s-automatic-differentiation-1.definition: Seppo Linnainmaa's 1970 master's thesis gave the first efficient representation of the derivative of a nested function, the reverse mode of automatic differentiation.
linnainmaa-s-automatic-differentiation-1.bottleneck: Before Linnainmaa's automatic differentiation, exact gradients of nested functions were impractical because numerical differentiation was inaccurate and symbolic differentiation blew up in expression size.

sources.title: The representation of the cumulative rounding error of an algorithm as a Taylor expansion of the local rounding errors

verification.notes: Date 1970 and the Q3 efficiency claim hold: reverse mode is asymptotically the tractable exact-gradient method for scalar-loss, many-parameter models, and Q1/Q2 pass mathematically. Weakness is paternity/causality: the Finnish thesis had no traceable influence on AI's adoption of backpropagation, which was independently re-derived by Werbos (1974) and Rumelhart et al. (1986), so Linnainmaa has priority but the transmission line to the parent is via reinvention.

attention-mechanism-bahdanau-2014.name: Attention mechanism (Bahdanau)
attention-mechanism-bahdanau-2014.definition: Bahdanau, Cho and Bengio introduced additive attention, letting a decoder dynamically focus on relevant source words during translation.
attention-mechanism-bahdanau-2014.bottleneck: Before the attention mechanism, neural sequence models were impractical on long inputs because a single fixed-length vector had to carry the entire source sequence.

sources.title: Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate - arXiv

verification.notes: Verified once across both edges (to the 2023 agent and to the 2017 Transformer). arXiv Sept 2014 date is correct (ICLR 2015) and Q2 holds: the Transformer directly generalizes this soft alignment to self-attention. Weakness: attention was concurrent, not solitary - Graves et al.'s Neural Turing Machine (2014) used content-based attention and Luong et al. (2015) supplied rival scoring forms - and Q1 shows long-sentence degradation relieved, i.e. improvement over a working fixed-vector baseline, not impossibility removed.

deep-residual-learning-resnet-2015-2015.name: Deep Residual Learning (ResNet) (2015)
deep-residual-learning-resnet-2015-2015.definition: He et al.'s residual learning framework where layers fit F(x)=H(x)-x and add their input back via identity shortcuts.
deep-residual-learning-resnet-2015-2015.bottleneck: Before deep residual learning, training very deep networks was impractical because added layers degraded accuracy through optimization difficulty rather than overfitting.

sources.title: Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition

verification.notes: Date Dec 2015 correct and before the 2017 Transformer, whose blocks do reuse identity shortcuts, so Q2 carries the gate. Clear multiple against Q3: Highway Networks (Srivastava, Greff & Schmidhuber, May 2015) trained very deep feedforward nets with gated skip connections seven months earlier and ResNet is its open-gate variant, a fact the ResNet paper acknowledges as concurrent work; Q1 was also only partial.

backpropagation-1986-1986.name: Backpropagation (1986)
backpropagation-1986-1986.definition: Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams' procedure for adjusting network weights by back-propagating output errors so hidden units learn representations.
backpropagation-1986-1986.bottleneck: Before backpropagation, training multilayer neural networks was impractical because there was no efficient general method for assigning credit to hidden units.

verification.notes: Date 1986 correct as the popularizing Rumelhart-Hinton-Williams paper and Q2 holds, but this is a textbook multiple/priority case: reverse-mode AD was published by Linnainmaa (1970), applied to networks by Werbos (1974/1982), and independently published by Parker and LeCun (1985). The 1986 node is a rediscovery and popularization, so necessity is 'the time was ripe', not sole invention.

sequence-to-sequence-learning-2014-2014.name: Sequence-to-sequence learning (2014)
sequence-to-sequence-learning-2014-2014.definition: Sutskever, Vinyals and Le's end-to-end encoder-decoder framework mapping an input sequence to an output sequence with LSTMs.
sequence-to-sequence-learning-2014-2014.bottleneck: Before sequence-to-sequence learning, mapping an input sequence to an output sequence of different length with one end-to-end neural model was impractical because models required fixed-size inputs and task-specific alignment structure.

sources.title: Sequence to Sequence Learning with Neural Networks

verification.notes: Date 2014 correct and Q2 holds: the Transformer inherited the encoder-decoder transduction framing. Clear multiple: Cho et al. (2014) independently proposed the RNN encoder-decoder the same year (EMNLP 2014), with Sutskever et al. adding deep LSTMs and input reversal, so seq2seq was a simultaneous invention; Q1 and Q3 were only partial in evaluation.

layer-normalization-2016-2016.name: Layer Normalization (2016)
layer-normalization-2016-2016.definition: Ba, Kiros and Hinton's normalization computing mean and variance over all summed inputs in a layer for a single training case.
layer-normalization-2016-2016.bottleneck: Before Layer Normalization, normalizing recurrent and sequence networks was impractical because batch statistics depended on sequence length and batch composition.

verification.notes: Date 2016 correct and before the 2017 Transformer, which does embed LayerNorm in every sub-layer, so Q2 as stated passes. Weakness: Q1/Q3 were only partial and ready substitutes exist - BatchNorm (2015) preceded it and RMSNorm (2019) has since replaced LayerNorm in many frontier LLMs (e.g. LLaMA), showing this specific normalization is replaceable rather than necessary.

neural-probabilistic-language-model-2003.name: Neural probabilistic language model (2003)
neural-probabilistic-language-model-2003.definition: Bengio and colleagues' 2003 model that learns a distributed vector representation for each word jointly with a neural probability function over word sequences.
neural-probabilistic-language-model-2003.bottleneck: Before the neural probabilistic language model, statistical language modeling was crippled by the curse of dimensionality because n-gram models treated words as discrete symbols with no notion of similarity between them.

verification.notes: Attacks fail: 2003 date is correct, no simultaneous rival neural language model jointly learning distributed word representations was found (earlier distributed representations were not a trained neural LM, and word2vec/GloVe came a decade later), and the causal line into embedding-based NLP and the Transformer's learned token embeddings is documented. Q1 was only partial, but Q2 independently and cleanly carries the gate.

napier-s-logarithms-1614-1614.name: Napier's logarithms (1614)
napier-s-logarithms-1614-1614.definition: Napier published logarithms in Mirifici Logarithmorum Canonis Descriptio (1614), turning multiplication into addition via precomputed tables.
napier-s-logarithms-1614-1614.bottleneck: Before Napier's logarithms, computing with products and powers of probabilities was impractical because multiplication of many small numbers had no additive representation.

verification.notes: 1614 publication date correct and Q2 holds (log-probability additivity underlies entropy/cross-entropy). Classic multiple against Q3: Jost Burgi independently invented logarithms (conceived c.1588, tables published 1620), as Britannica and MacTutor confirm, so logarithms were a parallel discovery and the time was ripe; Napier retains publication priority only.

boltzmann-s-entropy-formula-1877-1877.name: Boltzmann's entropy formula (1877)
boltzmann-s-entropy-formula-1877-1877.definition: Boltzmann in 1877 defined entropy as S = k log W, the logarithm of the number of microstates corresponding to a macrostate.
boltzmann-s-entropy-formula-1877-1877.bottleneck: Before Boltzmann's entropy formula, entropy had no probabilistic definition because macroscopic entropy was not connected to the logarithm of the number of microstates.

verification.notes: Q2 holds: the 1877 paper did establish entropy as proportional to the logarithm of a probability, the move Shannon generalized. Weakness is attribution of the formula itself: Boltzmann never wrote S = k log W or introduced the constant k - Planck wrote that form c.1900-01 and named it for him - so the node's named equation is anachronistic even though the 1877 conceptual contribution and date are real.

fisher-s-maximum-likelihood-estimation-1.name: Fisher's maximum likelihood estimation (1922)
fisher-s-maximum-likelihood-estimation-1.definition: Fisher's 1922 paper formalized choosing parameters that maximize the likelihood, in practice its logarithm, of the observed data under the model.
fisher-s-maximum-likelihood-estimation-1.bottleneck: Before Fisher's maximum likelihood estimation, fitting a model distribution to data lacked a principled objective because there was no general criterion identifying the parameters that make the observed data most probable.

verification.notes: Q1's identity (maximizing log-likelihood = minimizing cross-entropy under the empirical distribution) is mathematically sound and Q2 holds. Weakness: maximum likelihood had extensive pre-Fisher use by Lagrange, Laplace, Gauss, Thiele and Edgeworth, and Fisher's own work spans 1912-1922, so 1922 is systematization/naming rather than invention; also the equivalence to cross-entropy is retrospective, not a documented influence on Shannon 1948.

gibbs-s-statistical-mechanics-and-gibbs-.name: Gibbs's statistical mechanics and Gibbs entropy (1902)
gibbs-s-statistical-mechanics-and-gibbs-.definition: Gibbs's Elementary Principles in Statistical Mechanics (1902) systematized ensembles, with entropy as the negative average index of probability, -sum p log p in modern form.
gibbs-s-statistical-mechanics-and-gibbs-.bottleneck: Before Gibbs's statistical mechanics, entropy for an arbitrary probability distribution over states was undefined because entropy existed only for specific physical systems, not as -sum p log p over any distribution.

sources.title: Elementary Principles in Statistical Mechanics - Project Gutenberg

verification.notes: Attacks fail: the 1902 text does state entropy as -k sum p_i log p_i over an arbitrary ensemble distribution, no earlier general form was found (Boltzmann covers only the equiprobable special case, which Gibbs reduces to), the date is strictly before 1948, and Shannon's entropy is formally this quantity. The Boltzmann-versus-Gibbs contrast strengthens rather than undermines Q3.

hartley-s-logarithmic-measure-of-informa.name: Hartley's logarithmic measure of information (1928)
hartley-s-logarithmic-measure-of-informa.definition: Hartley's 1928 Transmission of Information quantified information as H = log S^n = n log S, the logarithm of the number of possible symbol sequences.
hartley-s-logarithmic-measure-of-informa.bottleneck: Before Hartley's logarithmic measure of information, the amount of information in a message had no quantitative measure because no one had defined information as proportional to the logarithm of the number of possible sequences.

verification.notes: Date 1928 correct, Shannon explicitly builds on Hartley, and Q2 holds, so the node survives. Weakness: Hartley's H = n log s covers only equiprobable symbols and rests on Nyquist's related 1924/1928 telegraph-transmission work, and the step that actually yields entropy/cross-entropy for arbitrary distributions is Shannon's 1948 generalization, making Hartley a genuine but partial precursor rather than the full measure.

huygens-s-expectation-1657-1657.name: Huygens's expectation (1657)
huygens-s-expectation-1657-1657.definition: Huygens's De Ratiociniis in Ludo Aleae (1657), the first printed probability textbook, formalized expectation as the probability-weighted value of an uncertain prospect.
huygens-s-expectation-1657-1657.bottleneck: Before Huygens's mathematical expectation, averaging a quantity over uncertain outcomes was impossible in principled form because probability had no expectation operator.

sources.title: Huygens - De Ratiociniis in Ludo Aleae (Dartmouth)

verification.notes: Q2 holds definitionally: cross-entropy is E_p[-log q] and Huygens 1657 is the first published treatise systematizing expectation. Weakness against Q3's 'no substitute in 1657': Pascal and Fermat had already explicitly calculated mathematical expectation in their 1654 correspondence (which Huygens learned of in Paris in 1655 and himself disclaimed priority for), so Huygens is first publisher/systematizer, not sole inventor.

raw_candidates.causal_claim: Transformer architecture made the modern AI agent possible by providing the scalable sequence model that all LLM cores are built on.

raw_candidates.name: Transformer architecture

raw_candidates.name: Self-attention mechanism

raw_candidates.name: Prolog
raw_candidates.source_title: The Birth of Prolog - Colmerauer & Roussel

raw_candidates.causal_claim: Turing Test proposal made the modern AI agent possible by framing machine intelligence as conversational behavior, the criterion chat-based agents are still implicitly judged against.

raw_candidates.name: Turing Test proposal

raw_candidates.causal_claim: McCulloch-Pitts neuron made the modern AI agent possible by supplying the first formal unit of neural computation from which all network models of learning descend.

raw_candidates.name: McCulloch-Pitts neuron
raw_candidates.source_title: A logical calculus of the ideas immanent in nervous activity - Bulletin of Mathematical Biophysics

raw_candidates.name: Speech recognition (Dragon NaturallySpeaking)

raw_candidates.name: Siri

raw_candidates.name: Watson (Jeopardy!)

candidate.causal_claim: Transformer architecture made the modern AI agent possible by providing the scalable sequence model that all LLM cores are built on.

candidate.name: Transformer architecture

candidate.causal_claim: Self-attention mechanism made the modern AI agent possible by letting its language core relate distant parts of a context in one parallel step, which recurrence could not do at scale.
candidate.definition: A mechanism that lets a model weigh the relevance of every token in a sequence against every other token in parallel, replacing sequential recurrence.
candidate.name: Self-attention mechanism

candidate.causal_claim: Attention mechanism (neural machine translation) made the modern AI agent possible by proving that learned soft alignment over context beats fixed-vector bottlenecks, the direct precursor of transformer self-attention.

candidate.name: Attention mechanism (neural machine translation)

candidate.causal_claim: Sequence-to-sequence learning made the modern AI agent possible by showing one trainable architecture could convert between arbitrary sequences, the template later generalized into prompt-to-response language modeling.

candidate.name: Sequence-to-sequence learning
candidate.source_title: Sequence to Sequence Learning with Neural Networks

candidate.name: Long short-term memory (LSTM)

candidate.name: Backpropagation popularized

candidate.causal_claim: Stochastic gradient descent made the modern AI agent possible by making it computationally feasible to optimize billions of parameters on streaming data, the training regime every LLM still uses.

candidate.name: Stochastic gradient descent
candidate.source_title: A Stochastic Approximation Method (Annals of Mathematical Statistics)

candidate.causal_claim: Adam optimizer made the modern AI agent possible by making transformer training stable and nearly tuning-free at scale, a practical precondition for fitting LLM cores.

candidate.name: Adam optimizer
candidate.source_title: Adam: A Method for Stochastic Optimization

candidate.causal_claim: Generative pre-training (GPT-1) made the modern AI agent possible by establishing the pretrain-then-adapt recipe that turns raw text into a general-purpose reasoning core.

candidate.name: Generative pre-training (GPT-1)

candidate.name: BERT masked language modeling
candidate.source_title: BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding

candidate.name: Scaling laws for neural language models
candidate.source_title: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models

candidate.name: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF)
candidate.source_title: Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback

candidate.causal_claim: Instruction tuning made the modern AI agent possible by making the model's interface plain language commands, the control surface every agent loop depends on.

candidate.name: Instruction tuning
candidate.source_title: Finetuned Language Models Are Zero-Shot Learners (FLAN)

candidate.causal_claim: Chain-of-thought prompting made the modern AI agent possible by showing an LLM can externalize step-by-step reasoning in language, the working-memory trick agent loops exploit for planning.

candidate.name: Chain-of-thought prompting
candidate.source_title: Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models

candidate.causal_claim: ReAct (reasoning and acting) made the modern AI agent possible by supplying the canonical reason-act-observe loop structure that defines the modern agent itself.

candidate.name: ReAct (reasoning and acting)
candidate.source_title: ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models

candidate.causal_claim: Byte-pair encoding tokenization made the modern AI agent possible by giving language models a robust way to convert arbitrary text into tokens, the perception front-end of every LLM core.

candidate.name: Byte-pair encoding tokenization
candidate.source_title: Neural Machine Translation of Rare Words with Subword Units

candidate.causal_claim: Word2vec embeddings made the modern AI agent possible by proving words and concepts can live as vectors a network can compute over, the representational assumption built into every transformer embedding layer.

candidate.name: Word2vec embeddings
candidate.source_title: Efficient Estimation of Word Representations in Vector Space

candidate.causal_claim: Distributional semantics (Firth's hypothesis) made the modern AI agent possible by supplying the theoretical license to learn meaning from raw text statistics alone, which is exactly what LLM pre-training does.
candidate.definition: The principle that a word's meaning is characterized by the company it keeps, i.e. by its distribution across contexts in text.
candidate.name: Distributional semantics (Firth's hypothesis)

candidate.causal_claim: CLIP vision-language model made the modern AI agent possible by giving agents a perception encoder that speaks the same representational language as their text core.
candidate.definition: A model trained contrastively on image-text pairs that aligns visual and linguistic representations in one embedding space, usable zero-shot.
candidate.name: CLIP vision-language model
candidate.source_title: Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision

candidate.causal_claim: Vision Transformer (ViT) made the modern AI agent possible by showing perception can run on the same transformer substrate as language, enabling one architecture to convert between modalities.
candidate.definition: Applying the pure transformer architecture to sequences of image patches, unifying vision with the same architecture used for language.
candidate.name: Vision Transformer (ViT)
candidate.source_title: An Image is Worth 16x16 Words: Transformers for Image Recognition at Scale

candidate.causal_claim: AlexNet made the modern AI agent possible by proving deep networks trained on GPUs decisively beat hand-engineered perception, starting the capability curve agents now ride.

candidate.name: AlexNet
candidate.source_title: ImageNet Classification with Deep Convolutional Neural Networks

candidate.causal_claim: ImageNet dataset made the modern AI agent possible by supplying the labeled data and benchmark that made perception trainable and comparable, the data pattern later repeated for language.

candidate.name: ImageNet dataset
candidate.source_title: ImageNet: A Large-Scale Hierarchical Image Database

candidate.causal_claim: CUDA made the modern AI agent possible by unlocking the massively parallel hardware without which transformer training at scale is computationally out of reach.

candidate.name: CUDA

candidate.causal_claim: Perceptron made the modern AI agent possible by originating the learnable-neuron paradigm from which every network inside an agent descends.
candidate.definition: Rosenblatt's first trainable artificial neural network, a machine that learned classification weights from examples.
candidate.name: Perceptron
candidate.source_title: The Perceptron: A Probabilistic Model for Information Storage and Organization in the Brain

candidate.causal_claim: Turing's learning machine proposal made the modern AI agent possible by first articulating that intelligence should be trained rather than programmed, the premise the entire agent program inherits.
candidate.definition: Turing's proposal in 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence' for child machines educated by reward and punishment instead of being fully programmed.
candidate.name: Turing's learning machine proposal

candidate.causal_claim: Information theory (Shannon) made the modern AI agent possible by founding the quantitative framework of information in which language modeling, cross-entropy loss and token prediction are defined.
candidate.definition: Shannon's mathematical theory of communication defining entropy and channel capacity, which made information a measurable quantity.
candidate.name: Information theory (Shannon)

candidate.causal_claim: Cross-entropy loss made the modern AI agent possible by giving language models their exact training signal: minimize surprise at the next token.
candidate.definition: The measure of divergence between a predicted probability distribution and the true one, derived from Shannon entropy and used as the standard training objective for classifiers and language models.
candidate.name: Cross-entropy loss

candidate.causal_claim: Maximum likelihood estimation made the modern AI agent possible by supplying the estimation principle that next-token training maximizes: the likelihood of real text under the model.
candidate.definition: Fisher's principle of choosing the parameters that make the observed data most probable, the statistical foundation of model fitting.
candidate.name: Maximum likelihood estimation

candidate.causal_claim: Bayesian probability (Bayes' theorem) made the modern AI agent possible by formalizing belief updating from evidence, the inferential stance probabilistic models and agent reasoning approximate.
candidate.definition: The rule for updating the probability of a hypothesis as evidence arrives, the formal backbone of reasoning under uncertainty.
candidate.name: Bayesian probability (Bayes' theorem)

candidate.causal_claim: Markov decision process formalism made the modern AI agent possible by defining the mathematical object an acting agent optimizes: a policy over states and actions with cumulative reward.

candidate.name: Markov decision process formalism

candidate.causal_claim: Q-learning made the modern AI agent possible by proving an agent can learn what to do purely from reward signals, the learning-from-feedback lineage that RLHF later adapted for language models.

candidate.name: Q-learning

candidate.causal_claim: Temporal difference learning made the modern AI agent possible by supplying the bootstrapped value-learning mechanism underlying the reinforcement methods used to align and steer agent behavior.

candidate.name: Temporal difference learning
candidate.source_title: Learning to Predict by the Methods of Temporal Differences

candidate.causal_claim: Monte Carlo tree search made the modern AI agent possible by demonstrating that learned models plus lookahead search produce superhuman sequential decisions, the planning pattern agent architectures imitate.
candidate.definition: A search algorithm that builds a decision tree guided by random simulation outcomes, famously powering AlphaGo's move selection.
candidate.name: Monte Carlo tree search

candidate.causal_claim: Statistical learning theory (VC dimension) made the modern AI agent possible by first making 'learning from finite data' a rigorous science, the intellectual frame in which training a model to generalize is understood.
candidate.definition: Vapnik and Chervonenkis's theory bounding generalization error by a capacity measure of a hypothesis class, founding the mathematics of learning from data.
candidate.name: Statistical learning theory (VC dimension)

candidate.causal_claim: Universal approximation theorem made the modern AI agent possible by guaranteeing that neural networks are expressive enough in principle to represent the mappings agents need, justifying the bet on scale.
candidate.definition: Cybenko's proof that a feedforward network with a single hidden layer can approximate any continuous function on a compact set.
candidate.name: Universal approximation theorem
candidate.source_title: Approximation by superpositions of a sigmoidal function

candidate.causal_claim: Stored-program architecture made the modern AI agent possible by creating the general-purpose computer on which every model, tool and agent loop physically runs.

candidate.name: Stored-program architecture

candidate.name: GLUE benchmark

candidate.causal_claim: GitHub made the modern AI agent possible by centralizing open-source collaboration, hosting the code, issues, and training corpora that the agent ecosystem is built from.

candidate.name: GitHub

candidate.causal_claim: The point-contact transistor made the modern AI agent possible by replacing vacuum tubes with a solid-state switch, the device from which all digital computing hardware descends.

candidate.name: Point-contact transistor

candidate.causal_claim: The silicon transistor made the modern AI agent possible by making transistors cheap, rugged, and manufacturable, turning computing hardware into a mass-produced commodity.

candidate.name: Silicon transistor

candidate.name: Planar process

candidate.definition: A set of electronic circuits on one small flat piece of semiconductor material, independently demonstrated by Kilby (1958) and Noyce (1959).
candidate.name: Integrated circuit

candidate.causal_claim: Photolithography made the modern AI agent possible by providing the printing technique that shrinks transistor features generation after generation.

candidate.name: Boolean algebra

candidate.definition: Linus Torvalds' free Unix-like operating system kernel, first released in 1991, now dominant in servers and supercomputing.
candidate.name: Linux operating system

candidate.causal_claim: Python made the modern AI agent possible by becoming the lingua franca in which the frameworks, experiments, and agent scaffolding are written.

candidate.name: Python (programming language)

candidate.causal_claim: arXiv made the modern AI agent possible by collapsing the delay between discovery and global scrutiny to days, letting agent techniques spread and compound at preprint speed.

candidate.name: arXiv

candidate.causal_claim: Wikipedia made the modern AI agent possible by creating a vast, structured, freely licensed text corpus that anchors language model knowledge and evaluation.

candidate.causal_claim: Bayesian network made the modern AI agent possible by formalizing probabilistic reasoning over structured variables, the statistics-derived framework for decision-making under uncertainty that agent planning builds on.

candidate.name: AlphaGo

candidate.causal_claim: Dropout made the modern AI agent possible by making very large networks trainable without catastrophic overfitting, a precondition for scaling to LLM size.

candidate.name: Dropout

candidate.causal_claim: Attention mechanism (Bahdanau) made the modern AI agent possible by introducing learned soft alignment over context, the mechanism transformers later generalized into self-attention.

candidate.name: Attention mechanism (Bahdanau)

candidate.causal_claim: ReAct agent pattern made the modern AI agent possible by defining the reason-act-observe loop that is the literal architecture of today's LLM agents.

candidate.causal_claim: ELIZA made the modern AI agent possible by demonstrating that humans will interact with machines conversationally through natural language, the interaction premise of every chat-based agent.

candidate.causal_claim: Lisp programming language made the modern AI agent possible by creating the symbolic-programming substrate in which the first agent-like reasoning systems were built and prototyped.
candidate.definition: John McCarthy's Lisp introduced symbolic list processing, recursion and garbage collection as the native medium of early AI research.
candidate.name: Lisp programming language
candidate.source_title: Recursive Functions of Symbolic Expressions and Their Computation by Machine, Part I - ACM

candidate.causal_claim: Logic Theorist made the modern AI agent possible by demonstrating that a machine could carry out heuristic search over symbolic goals, the first concrete instance of automated reasoning.
candidate.definition: Newell, Shaw and Simon's Logic Theorist was the first program designed to mimic human problem-solving, proving theorems from Principia Mathematica.
candidate.name: Logic Theorist
candidate.source_title: The Logic Theory Machine - Newell & Simon (1956)

candidate.causal_claim: Dartmouth Workshop made the modern AI agent possible by founding artificial intelligence as an organized research field whose research programs produced every later agent technology.
candidate.definition: The 1956 Dartmouth summer workshop coined 'artificial intelligence' and convened the field's founders around the conjecture that intelligence can be simulated by machines.
candidate.name: Dartmouth Workshop
candidate.source_title: A Proposal for the Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence

candidate.causal_claim: Expert systems (DENDRAL/MYCIN) made the modern AI agent possible by proving machines could be deployed as task-performing knowledge agents, the commercial ancestor of today's task agents.
candidate.definition: DENDRAL and later MYCIN encoded expert knowledge as rule bases that could reason about chemistry and medical diagnosis at expert level in narrow domains.
candidate.name: Expert systems (DENDRAL/MYCIN)

candidate.causal_claim: Prolog made the modern AI agent possible by showing declarative goal-directed inference could be mechanized, a direct ancestor of the goal-and-plan machinery in agent architectures.
candidate.definition: Prolog is a logic programming language built on Horn clauses, where programs state facts and rules and the interpreter performs automated inference.
candidate.name: Prolog
candidate.source_title: The Birth of Prolog - Colmerauer & Roussel

candidate.causal_claim: Turing Test proposal made the modern AI agent possible by framing machine intelligence as conversational behavior, the criterion chat-based agents are still implicitly judged against.
candidate.definition: Alan Turing's 1950 paper proposed the imitation game as an operational test of machine intelligence and anticipated learning machines.
candidate.name: Turing Test proposal

candidate.causal_claim: McCulloch-Pitts neuron made the modern AI agent possible by supplying the first formal unit of neural computation from which all network models of learning descend.
candidate.definition: McCulloch and Pitts modeled neurons as threshold logic units, the first mathematical model of an artificial neural network.
candidate.name: McCulloch-Pitts neuron
candidate.source_title: A logical calculus of the ideas immanent in nervous activity - Bulletin of Mathematical Biophysics

candidate.causal_claim: General Problem Solver made the modern AI agent possible by introducing means-ends analysis, the goal-directed planning schema that agent architectures still instantiate.
candidate.definition: Newell, Shaw and Simon's General Problem Solver attacked problems by means-ends analysis, reducing differences between current and goal states.
candidate.name: General Problem Solver
candidate.source_title: Report on a general problem-solving program - ACM Digital Library

candidate.causal_claim: Deep Blue made the modern AI agent possible by proving a machine could out-perform the best human at a flagship intellectual task through search, legitimizing machine agency in adversarial domains.
candidate.definition: IBM's Deep Blue defeated world champion Garry Kasparov using massively parallel alpha-beta search and hand-tuned evaluation.
candidate.name: Deep Blue

candidate.causal_claim: TD-Gammon made the modern AI agent possible by first proving an agent can reach expert performance by learning from its own experience, the self-improvement loop at the heart of RL-trained agents.
candidate.definition: Tesauro's TD-Gammon learned world-class backgammon play purely by self-play temporal-difference reinforcement learning.
candidate.name: TD-Gammon
candidate.source_title: Practical Issues in Temporal Difference Learning - Springer

candidate.causal_claim: Speech recognition (Dragon NaturallySpeaking) made the modern AI agent possible by opening the voice channel through which users now direct agents hands-free.
candidate.definition: Dragon NaturallySpeaking was the first general-purpose continuous speech recognition product for dictation on personal computers.
candidate.name: Speech recognition (Dragon NaturallySpeaking)

candidate.causal_claim: Siri made the modern AI agent possible by normalizing the consumer expectation of a conversational assistant that takes actions on your behalf, the market category LLM agents now fulfill.
candidate.definition: Apple's Siri brought a voice-controlled personal assistant that interprets natural language and delegates to services to a mass consumer device.
candidate.name: Siri

candidate.causal_claim: Watson (Jeopardy!) made the modern AI agent possible by demonstrating machine question-answering over open-domain natural language at champion level, a direct functional precursor of knowledge agents.
candidate.definition: IBM Watson defeated Jeopardy! champions by combining massive evidence retrieval with probabilistic answer scoring over unstructured text.
candidate.name: Watson (Jeopardy!)
candidate.source_title: This is Watson - IBM Journal of Research and Development

raw_candidates.causal_claim: Long Short-Term Memory made the Transformer architecture possible by proving long-range sequence dependencies could be learned, defining the long-context problem whose sequential, non-parallel training the Transformer then removed.
raw_candidates.definition: A gated recurrent network by Hochreiter and Schmidhuber that preserves error flow over more than 1,000 time steps.
raw_candidates.name: Long Short-Term Memory (1997)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: Sequence-to-sequence learning made the Transformer architecture possible by supplying the encoder-decoder template the Transformer kept, while its fixed-vector bottleneck and sequential LSTM encoding motivated replacing recurrence with attention.
raw_candidates.definition: Sutskever, Vinyals and Le's end-to-end encoder-decoder framework mapping an input sequence to an output sequence with LSTMs.
raw_candidates.name: Sequence-to-sequence learning (2014)
raw_candidates.source_title: Sequence to Sequence Learning with Neural Networks

raw_candidates.causal_claim: Attention mechanism (Bahdanau) made the Transformer architecture possible by showing a model could dispense with a single fixed-length vector and instead weight all source positions, the operation the Transformer generalized into self-attention as its sole sequence mixer.
raw_candidates.definition: Bahdanau, Cho and Bengio's soft alignment that lets a decoder form a fresh weighted sum of encoder states for each output word.
raw_candidates.name: Attention mechanism (Bahdanau) (2014)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: Gated Recurrent Unit made the Transformer architecture possible by demonstrating in the 2014 encoder-decoder translation systems that gated units captured long dependencies, sharpening the state of the art whose sequential computation the Transformer had to beat in parallel.
raw_candidates.definition: Cho et al.'s simplified gated recurrent unit with update and reset gates, comparable to LSTM with fewer parameters.
raw_candidates.name: Gated Recurrent Unit (2014)
raw_candidates.source_title: Empirical Evaluation of Gated Recurrent Neural Networks on Sequence Modeling

raw_candidates.causal_claim: ByteNet made the Transformer architecture possible by proving a non-recurrent, parallelizable convolutional sequence model could beat recurrent translation models, directly attacking the RNN serial bottleneck the Transformer also removed.
raw_candidates.definition: Kalchbrenner et al.'s dilated convolutional encoder-decoder for translation that runs in linear time and preserves temporal resolution.
raw_candidates.name: ByteNet (2016)
raw_candidates.source_title: Neural Machine Translation in Linear Time

raw_candidates.causal_claim: Word2vec embeddings made the Transformer architecture possible by establishing learned dense token embeddings as the standard input representation, which the Transformer adopts as its embedding layer added to positional encodings.
raw_candidates.definition: Mikolov et al.'s efficient CBOW and skip-gram methods for learning dense continuous word vectors from billions of words.
raw_candidates.name: Word2vec embeddings (2013)
raw_candidates.source_title: Efficient Estimation of Word Representations in Vector Space

raw_candidates.causal_claim: Deep Residual Learning (ResNet) made the Transformer architecture possible by supplying the residual shortcut connections wrapped around every Transformer sub-layer, enabling deep stacks to train without degradation.
raw_candidates.definition: He et al.'s residual learning framework where layers fit F(x)=H(x)-x and add their input back via identity shortcuts.
raw_candidates.name: Deep Residual Learning (ResNet) (2015)
raw_candidates.source_title: Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition

raw_candidates.causal_claim: Layer Normalization made the Transformer architecture possible by providing the per-example normalization used in every Transformer block to stabilize hidden dynamics independent of batch size.
raw_candidates.definition: Ba, Kiros and Hinton's normalization computing mean and variance over all summed inputs in a layer for a single training case.
raw_candidates.name: Layer Normalization (2016)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: Dropout made the Transformer architecture possible by providing the regularization applied in its attention, feed-forward and residual paths, allowing a large translation model to generalize from WMT data.
raw_candidates.definition: Srivastava et al.'s regularization that randomly drops units during training to prevent co-adaptation and overfitting.
raw_candidates.name: Dropout (2014)
raw_candidates.source_title: Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting

raw_candidates.causal_claim: GloVe made the Transformer architecture possible by reinforcing that token meaning lives in a learned vector space structured by dot products, the same dot-product geometry the Transformer's scaled dot-product attention and embeddings exploit.
raw_candidates.definition: Pennington, Socher and Manning's global log-bilinear regression model learning word vectors from global co-occurrence counts.
raw_candidates.name: GloVe (2014)
raw_candidates.source_title: Glove: Global Vectors for Word Representation

raw_candidates.causal_claim: Cross-entropy loss made the Transformer architecture possible by giving its softmax output over the vocabulary a principled training objective, so next-token and translation training is maximum-likelihood estimation.
raw_candidates.definition: The expected cost of encoding data from distribution p with a code optimized for model q, equal to negative log-likelihood as a training loss.
raw_candidates.name: Cross-entropy loss (1948)
raw_candidates.source_title: Cross-Entropy and the Cross-Entropy Loss – AI in Action

raw_candidates.causal_claim: Gradient descent made the Transformer architecture possible by supplying the first-order optimization principle, in stochastic and Adam variants, by which all Transformer parameters are trained.
raw_candidates.definition: Cauchy's iterative method for minimizing a function by stepping in the direction of the negative gradient.
raw_candidates.name: Gradient descent (1847)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: Linnainmaa's automatic differentiation made the Transformer architecture possible by providing the reverse-mode gradient computation implemented in modern frameworks that train the Transformer's attention projections.
raw_candidates.definition: Linnainmaa's reverse mode of automatic differentiation, computing derivatives of nested differentiable functions by propagating errors backward through a graph.
raw_candidates.name: Linnainmaa's automatic differentiation (1970)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: Backpropagation made the Transformer architecture possible by making end-to-end training of deep multi-layer networks practical, including jointly training attention alignment with the rest of the model as later Transformer training requires.
raw_candidates.definition: Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams' procedure for adjusting network weights by back-propagating output errors so hidden units learn representations.
raw_candidates.name: Backpropagation (1986)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: A Mathematical Theory of Communication made the Transformer architecture possible by founding the probabilistic view of language as a distribution over symbols, from which the Transformer's softmax probabilities, entropy and perplexity evaluation derive.
raw_candidates.definition: Shannon's founding information theory introducing entropy as the measure of uncertainty and the limits of lossless encoding.
raw_candidates.name: A Mathematical Theory of Communication (1948)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: CUDA made the Transformer architecture possible by exposing thousands of GPU cores for the dense matrix multiplications of attention, making parallel-over-sequence training computationally feasible.
raw_candidates.definition: NVIDIA's parallel computing platform and API, released February 16, 2007, letting GPUs be used for general-purpose computation.
raw_candidates.name: CUDA (2007)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: TensorFlow made the Transformer architecture possible by providing the dataflow framework with automatic differentiation and GPU distribution in which the original Transformer was implemented and trained.
raw_candidates.definition: Google Brain's open-source machine learning system, released November 9, 2015, for expressing and executing dataflow computations on heterogeneous hardware.
raw_candidates.name: TensorFlow (2015)
raw_candidates.source_title: TensorFlow: Large-Scale Machine Learning on Heterogeneous Distributed Systems

raw_candidates.causal_claim: ImageNet made the Transformer architecture possible by proving large labeled benchmarks plus GPU training could drive deep-network breakthroughs, creating the benchmark-and-scale culture and GPU practice later applied to translation.
raw_candidates.definition: Deng et al.'s large-scale hierarchical image database of 3.2 million images in 5,247 WordNet synsets presented at CVPR 2009.
raw_candidates.name: ImageNet (2009)
raw_candidates.source_title: ImageNet: A Large-Scale Hierarchical Image Database

raw_candidates.causal_claim: WMT made the Transformer architecture possible by supplying the standardized WMT'14 English-German and English-French benchmarks on which the Transformer was defined and claimed state of the art.
raw_candidates.definition: The first WMT workshop and shared translation task, held in 2006, comparing machine translation systems on common Europarl data.
raw_candidates.name: WMT Workshop on Statistical Machine Translation (2006)
raw_candidates.source_title: Ten Years of WMT Evaluation Campaigns: Lessons Learnt

raw_candidates.causal_claim: BLEU score made the Transformer architecture possible by giving translation research a cheap, reproducible yardstick, the exact metric the Transformer paper used to demonstrate superiority over recurrent and convolutional models.
raw_candidates.definition: Papineni et al.'s automatic machine translation metric based on clipped n-gram precision against human references with a brevity penalty.
raw_candidates.name: BLEU score (2002)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: Penn Treebank made the Transformer architecture possible by pioneering large tokenized, annotated text corpora as training and test material for statistical language models, the substrate paradigm sequence models including Transformers depend on.
raw_candidates.definition: Marcus, Santorini and Marcinkiewicz's corpus of over 4.5 million words of American English annotated with part-of-speech tags and skeletal syntax.
raw_candidates.name: Penn Treebank (1993)
raw_candidates.source_title: Building a Large Annotated Corpus of English: The Penn Treebank

raw_candidates.causal_claim: Europarl corpus made the Transformer architecture possible by providing the sentence-aligned parallel text that trained and evaluated the WMT translation pipeline from which the Transformer's task, data format and baselines came.
raw_candidates.definition: Koehn's parallel corpus of European Parliament proceedings in 11 languages, about 30 million words per language, for statistical machine translation.
raw_candidates.name: Europarl corpus (2005)
raw_candidates.source_title: Europarl: A Parallel Corpus for Statistical Machine Translation

raw_candidates.causal_claim: Common Crawl made the Transformer architecture possible by creating a freely available web-scale text substrate, demonstrating that massive raw corpora could be collected and shared for training data-hungry sequence models.
raw_candidates.definition: A nonprofit founded in 2007 by Gil Elbaz that crawls the web and freely provides petabyte-scale archives of web pages to the public.
raw_candidates.name: Common Crawl (2007)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: One Billion Word Benchmark made the Transformer architecture possible by normalizing billion-word tokenized corpora and perplexity comparison at scale, showing sequence models improved with data volume as Transformer training assumes.
raw_candidates.definition: Chelba et al.'s benchmark corpus with almost one billion words of training data for measuring progress in statistical language modeling.
raw_candidates.name: One Billion Word Benchmark (2013)
raw_candidates.source_title: One Billion Word Benchmark for Measuring Progress in Statistical Language Modeling

raw_candidates.causal_claim: BookCorpus made the Transformer architecture possible by providing long, contiguous narrative text suitable for learning sentence and long-context representations, the kind of long-sequence material recurrent models struggled with and Transformers were built to exploit.
raw_candidates.definition: Zhu et al.'s dataset of around 11,038 free books containing 984 million words, introduced for aligning books and movies.
raw_candidates.name: BookCorpus (2015)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: Bayes' theorem made the Transformer architecture possible by supplying the conditional-probability calculus in which next-token prediction, the Transformer's training task, is formulated.
raw_candidates.definition: A rule for computing a conditional probability distribution from a prior distribution and the likelihood of observed evidence.
raw_candidates.name: Bayes' theorem (1763)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: Matrix algebra (Cayley) made the Transformer architecture possible by defining the matrix multiplication from which every query, key, value and feed-forward computation in a Transformer block is built.
raw_candidates.definition: Arthur Cayley's 1858 memoir gave the first abstract definition of a matrix and defined matrix addition, multiplication, scalar multiplication and inverses.
raw_candidates.name: Matrix algebra (Cayley) (1858)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: Gradient descent made the Transformer architecture possible by providing the optimization principle used to fit its millions of weights to a language-modeling loss.
raw_candidates.definition: Augustin-Louis Cauchy's 1847 iterative method for minimizing a differentiable function by stepping in the direction of the negative gradient.
raw_candidates.name: Gradient descent (1847)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: Boltzmann distribution made the Transformer architecture possible by giving the exponential-normalized form that the softmax in its attention weights and output layer directly instantiates, with scores in place of energies.
raw_candidates.definition: Ludwig Boltzmann's 1868 probability distribution assigning each state a probability proportional to the exponential of its negative energy divided by temperature.
raw_candidates.name: Boltzmann distribution (1868)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: Cross-entropy loss made the Transformer architecture possible by serving as the exact objective minimized when a Transformer is trained to predict the next token.
raw_candidates.definition: The information-theoretic measure, rooted in Claude Shannon's 1948 theory, of the average negative log-probability a predicted distribution assigns to outcomes drawn from a target distribution.
raw_candidates.name: Cross-entropy loss (1948)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: GeForce 256 made the Transformer architecture possible by establishing the GPU as a distinct parallel processor class, the hardware lineage whose dense matrix throughput Transformers require because they abandoned sequential recurrence for parallel matrix operations.
raw_candidates.definition: NVIDIA's 1999 GeForce 256, marketed as the world's first GPU, a single-chip processor with integrated transform, lighting, triangle setup and rendering engines.
raw_candidates.name: GeForce 256 (1999)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: arXiv made the Transformer architecture possible by creating the rapid preprint channel through which its predecessor results in attention, sequence-to-sequence learning and optimization circulated and on which 'Attention Is All You Need' itself was first published.
raw_candidates.definition: Paul Ginsparg's open-access preprint repository, launched on August 14, 1991 at Los Alamos, for circulating scientific papers before journal publication.
raw_candidates.name: arXiv (1991)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: Amazon EC2 made the Transformer architecture possible by making large fleets of rented compute, including GPU instances, available on demand, so training a compute-hungry parallel architecture no longer required owning a supercomputer.
raw_candidates.definition: Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud, launched in public beta on August 25, 2006, which lets users rent virtual computers by the hour to run their own applications.
raw_candidates.name: Amazon EC2 (2006)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: CUDA made the Transformer architecture possible by exposing GPU parallelism to general code, and the Transformer's design bet — replacing sequential recurrence with large parallelizable matrix multiplications — only pays off on CUDA-programmable hardware.
raw_candidates.definition: NVIDIA's parallel computing platform and API, officially released in February 2007, that lets software use GPUs for general-purpose accelerated processing.
raw_candidates.name: CUDA (2007)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: TensorFlow made the Transformer architecture possible by providing the automatic-differentiation, GPU and distributed-training framework in which the original Transformer was implemented and trained at Google.
raw_candidates.definition: Google Brain's open-source machine learning library, released under the Apache 2.0 license on November 9, 2015, for expressing and executing dataflow computations on heterogeneous hardware.
raw_candidates.name: TensorFlow (2015)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: Broadbent's filter model of attention made the Transformer architecture possible by originating the psychology concept of attention as selective allocation of limited processing capacity that neural attention mechanisms, and hence the Transformer, borrowed by name and function.
raw_candidates.definition: Donald Broadbent's 1958 early-selection theory that a selective filter admits only one channel of sensory information into a limited-capacity processing system.
raw_candidates.name: Broadbent's filter model of attention (1958)

raw_candidates.causal_claim: Hubel and Wiesel receptive fields made the Transformer architecture possible by establishing the hierarchical feature-detection model of cortex that inspired convolutional and layered neural architectures, the vision tradition from which multi-head attention's multiple parallel feature channels descend.
raw_candidates.definition: David Hubel and Torsten Wiesel's 1962 finding that visual cortex neurons respond selectively to oriented edges, with simple cells built from aligned inputs and complex cells pooling simple cells.
raw_candidates.name: Hubel and Wiesel receptive fields (1962)
raw_candidates.source_title: Neural Mechanisms for the Generation of Visual Complex Cells

raw_candidates.causal_claim: IBM Models of statistical machine translation made the Transformer architecture possible by formalizing alignment between source and target words as a probabilistic object, the direct ancestor of the learned soft alignments that became attention in neural translation and then self-attention.
raw_candidates.definition: Brown and colleagues' 1993 series of five statistical translation models that define a word-by-word alignment between sentence pairs and assign a probability to each alignment.
raw_candidates.name: IBM Models of statistical machine translation (1993)
raw_candidates.source_title: The Mathematics of Statistical Machine Translation: Parameter Estimation

raw_candidates.causal_claim: Posner cueing paradigm made the Transformer architecture possible by demonstrating experimentally that attention is a movable, measurable allocation that can be directed to a location before a stimulus arrives, the cognitive framing later formalized as query-driven attention weighting in the Transformer.
raw_candidates.definition: Michael Posner's 1980 'Orienting of Attention' paradigm measuring, via valid and invalid spatial cues, how covertly shifting attention speeds or slows target detection.
raw_candidates.name: Posner cueing paradigm (1980)
raw_candidates.source_title: ORIENTING OF ATTENTION: THEN AND NOW

raw_candidates.causal_claim: Attention mechanism (Bahdanau) made the Transformer architecture possible by proving that learned soft alignment weights could replace a fixed-length sentence vector; the Transformer generalized that alignment into self-attention and discarded the recurrent encoder-decoder around it.

candidate.causal_claim: Briggs's Arithmetica Logarithmica made cross-entropy loss possible by making logarithms a cheap table lookup, so log-probability scores could actually be computed by hand.

candidate.causal_claim: The Pascaline made cross-entropy loss possible by proving repeated arithmetic over many numbers could be mechanized, a precondition for summing log-losses over datasets.

candidate.causal_claim: Babbage's Difference Engine made cross-entropy loss possible by pursuing error-free automated table computation, the calculation infrastructure needed to evaluate losses at scale.
candidate.definition: Babbage announced the Difference Engine in 1822 to automate computation and printing of mathematical tables, especially logarithm tables for navigation.

candidate.causal_claim: The Hollerith tabulating machine made cross-entropy loss possible by mechanizing counting of categorical outcomes into frequency distributions, the empirical distributions cross-entropy is computed from.
candidate.definition: Hollerith's electromechanical punched-card tabulator processed the 1890 US census, counting cards by category far faster than hand tabulation.
candidate.name: Hollerith tabulating machine (1890)

candidate.causal_claim: Kepler's Rudolphine Tables made cross-entropy loss possible by showing printed tables of predicted positions could be checked against observed reality, the prediction-versus-reality substrate of a loss.

candidate.causal_claim: Graunt's Observations made cross-entropy loss possible by first turning raw counts into an empirical probability distribution over outcomes, the target distribution in cross-entropy.
candidate.definition: Graunt's 1662 analysis of London's Bills of Mortality produced the first life table, turning parish death records into survival proportions.

candidate.definition: Halley published in 1693 a life table from Breslau birth and death records for 1687-1691 and used it to price life annuities by age.

candidate.causal_claim: Quetelet's Sur l'homme made cross-entropy loss possible by showing whole populations form concrete normal distributions in printed data, extending distributional thinking from errors to real categorical and measured populations.
candidate.definition: Quetelet's Sur l'homme (1835) applied the normal distribution to measured human traits in large populations, centred on the homme moyen or average man.

candidate.causal_claim: Leibniz's differential calculus made cross-entropy loss possible by providing differentiation for minimising a loss function with respect to model parameters.

candidate.name: Leibniz's differential calculus (1684)

candidate.causal_claim: Kolmogorov's probability axioms made cross-entropy loss possible by giving predicted and true distributions the rigorous measure-theoretic form cross-entropy compares.

candidate.name: Kolmogorov's probability axioms (1933)

candidate.causal_claim: Mersenne's Académie Parisienne made cross-entropy loss possible by circulating the gambling problems and letters from which probability and expectation emerged.
candidate.definition: Marin Mersenne set up the informal Académie Parisienne in 1635, a correspondence network of nearly 140 scholars including Pascal and Fermat.
candidate.name: Mersenne's Académie Parisienne (1635)

candidate.causal_claim: The Royal Society made cross-entropy loss possible by creating a durable institution that published and arbitrated probability work from Huygens to Bayes and Fisher.
candidate.definition: The Royal Society was founded on 28 November 1660 at Gresham College, London, as a college for promoting physico-mathematical experimental learning.
candidate.name: The Royal Society (1660)

candidate.causal_claim: Journal des Sçavans made cross-entropy loss possible by inventing the dated scholarly journal through which mathematical results could spread and be cited across Europe.

candidate.causal_claim: Philosophical Transactions made cross-entropy loss possible by providing the venue that published Halley's life table in 1693 and Bayes's essay in 1763.

candidate.name: Philosophical Transactions (1665)
candidate.source_title: About | Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A

candidate.causal_claim: French Academy of Sciences made cross-entropy loss possible by sustaining the Paris mathematical community that produced Laplace's probability theory and least-squares work.

candidate.name: French Academy of Sciences (1666)

candidate.causal_claim: Cardano's Liber de Ludo Aleae made cross-entropy loss possible by importing counting of gambling outcomes into mathematics as the first systematic notion of probability.
candidate.definition: Gerolamo Cardano wrote Liber de Ludo Aleae around 1564, defining probability as the ratio of favourable to total possible outcomes for dice games.

candidate.causal_claim: Pascal-Fermat correspondence made cross-entropy loss possible by founding mathematical probability, without which no predicted distribution could be defined or scored.
candidate.definition: Blaise Pascal and Pierre de Fermat corresponded in 1654 on the problem of points, establishing expectation and combinatorial probability.
candidate.name: Pascal-Fermat correspondence (1654)
candidate.source_title: Probability and statistics | History, Examples, & Facts | Britannica

candidate.causal_claim: de Moivre's Doctrine of Chances made cross-entropy loss possible by supplying the binomial distribution and its normal approximation that classifiers later model and score.
candidate.definition: Abraham de Moivre published The Doctrine of Chances in 1718, the first textbook on probability theory; its 1738 edition introduced the normal approximation to the binomial.
candidate.name: de Moivre's Doctrine of Chances (1718)

candidate.causal_claim: Bayes's Essay made cross-entropy loss possible by giving the rule for inverting conditional probabilities, linking observed data to a posterior distribution over hypotheses.
candidate.definition: Thomas Bayes's Essay towards solving a Problem in the Doctrine of Chances was read at the Royal Society on 23 December 1763 and published in Philosophical Transactions.
